tldr: This paper measures latency bottlenecks in VLAs, uncovers the trajectory characteristics of Flow Matching, cuts denoising down to just 2 steps (21.96 ms), and evaluates real-time execution methods on physical robots using a newly built concurrent framework.
hero_caption: Timescale mismatch between VLA inference and robot control. Synchronous inference introduces stalls waiting for model computation, while naive asynchronous execution leads to stale observations and boundary discontinuities across chunk transitions.
overview:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models hold strong promise as general-purpose robot policies. However, deploying them on physical robots reveals a severe timescale gap: inference is too slow to match robot control rates. To bridge the gap between low-rate inference (a few Hz) and high-rate control (hundreds of Hz), most systems rely on asynchronous execution and action chunking. Yet, stacked delays—from observation capture and inference to communication and physical robot response—cause the executed action to diverge from the actual environmental state.

In this work, the authors first dissect and measure end-to-end latency across camera exposure, readout, proprioception, communication, physical response, and model inference. They find that repeated Flow Matching denoising is a primary bottleneck on the model side, and that its velocity field stays relatively stable during early to intermediate stages before concentrating sharp directional corrections near the end. Based on this stage heterogeneity, they propose two-stage non-uniform denoising: instead of uniform time steps, it uses a large coarse step first and then refines a short terminal segment with SnapFlow. This reduces the number of function evaluations (NFE) from 10 to 2, slashing model-inference time from 61.56 ms to 21.96 ms.

Furthermore, the authors develop a distributed real-time VLA framework that completely decouples the rates of inference, action publication, and robot control. Evaluating six representative real-time execution methods under identical conditions on a challenging bimanual garment-folding task, they show that Legato leads among training-based methods and Temporal Smoothing performs best among training-free methods in terms of success rate and trajectory smoothness. Combining either method with the proposed two-step Flow Matching yields dramatic inference speedups while preserving high task performance.
contributions: Established a calibration procedure to comprehensively measure and quantify end-to-end latency sources, ranging from camera exposure and readout to joint response and VLA model inference.

Uncovered the terminal-correction characteristic of the Flow Matching velocity field, reducing inference time by about 64% using a two-stage non-uniform 2-step (2-NFE) denoising scheme that pairs long-interval generation with short-interval refinement.

Developed an open-source distributed real-time VLA framework that separates inference, publication, and control loops across threads and processes, enabling unified benchmarking and provenance tracking of real-time execution methods.
Systematically compared six real-time execution methods on a bimanual garment-folding task, clarifying the tradeoffs across trajectory continuity, acceleration smoothness, and task throughput.

sections.heading: Why Do VLAs Fall Behind on Real Robots? The Timescale Mismatch
sections.summary: A large timing gap exists between the high generalization power of VLAs and the high-frequency control requirements of physical robots. Even with asynchronous execution, issues like stale observations and chunk-boundary discontinuities remain, and systematic latency profiling or unified benchmarking has been lacking.
sections.details:
VLA models are a compelling path toward general-purpose robot control, but their heavy computational demands create a fundamental mismatch with the high-frequency control loops (tens to hundreds of Hz) required by physical hardware. Common workarounds include action chunking, which predicts multi-step trajectories at once, and asynchronous execution, which runs background inference concurrently while the robot executes previously generated actions.

However, these strategies do not fully solve the problem. Because a new chunk is generated from an observation captured when inference started, boundaries between chunks suffer from inter-chunk discontinuity, while the executing actions drift from the evolving real world (intra-chunk inconsistency). In addition, system-level delays such as camera exposure, image transmission, communication, and physical joint response compound the issue. Achieving real-time operation is therefore an end-to-end challenge, not just a matter of making the model smaller.

Prior work has explored distillation, step reduction, trajectory splining, executed-prefix conditioning, and latency forecasting. Yet, differing base models, hardware setups, and evaluation tasks have made direct comparisons difficult. Moreover, the exact role played by each step inside Flow Matching remained poorly understood. To address this, this paper uses $\pi_{0.5}$ as a baseline to measure latency, overhaul the denoising mechanism, and benchmark methods on a real robot under a unified framework.

sections.heading: Pinpointing Delays: Profiling System Latency and Model Inference
sections.summary: Full latency profiling on a physical robot shows that perception, communication, and hardware response alone consume tens of milliseconds. On the model side, iterative Flow Matching sampling accounts for the bulk of inference time.
sections.details:
### 2.1 End-to-End Timeline and Non-Model Delays
Before a robot executes a new action, data traverses a lengthy pipeline: image exposure, frame readout, state feedback, preprocessing, inference dispatch, model computation, result return, buffering, and physical response. To profile this, the authors built a calibration rig where a RealSense camera records both a high-precision on-screen timecode and an ArUco marker on the robot gripper while the arm moves in a sinusoidal pattern.

Measurements revealed a camera timestamp offset of 17.69 ms, an image readout delay of 32.82 ms, proprioceptive feedback latency of 26.4 ± 6.2 ms, and an actuation response delay of 15.3 ± 5.4 ms before commanded motion actually begins. Non-model sources alone easily add up to nearly 80 ms of latency, proving that speeding up the model alone cannot eliminate synchronization issues with the physical world.

### 2.2 Model Inference Breakdown
The inference time of a Flow Matching VLA splits into a fixed cost for image and language feature encoding ($T_{\mathrm{cond}}$) and an iterative step cost in the action head ($T_{\mathrm{step}}^{(k)}$). On an NVIDIA RTX 4090 D, standard 10-step (10-NFE) sampling took 61.56 ms on average. Reducing the number of sampling steps was therefore identified as the primary lever for accelerating the model.

captions.F2: Integrated calibration apparatus and measurement pipeline for system latency. By capturing both the on-screen timecode and the end-effector marker with the camera and aligning them with host logs, delays such as image readout and joint response are isolated with millisecond precision.

sections.heading: From 10 Steps to 2: Stage-Aware Non-Uniform Flow Denoising
sections.summary: Analyzing Flow Matching trajectories revealed that the velocity field is steady in magnitude and direction early on, with sharp directional adjustments concentrated near the end. Exploiting this, the authors propose a non-uniform two-step method that traverses most of the interval in one step and uses SnapFlow for fine-grained terminal correction.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Stage Heterogeneity of the Velocity Field
Standard Flow Matching sampling using Euler integration divides time into uniform steps. However, examining velocity vectors $v_k$ during 10-step inference shows that both root-mean-square (RMS) magnitude changes and angular deviations $\theta_k$ between adjacent steps remain very small and stable from steps 1 through 8. Only at the very end, in steps 9 and 10, does the angular change spike, indicating aggressive directional corrections. This suggests that taking a large coarse step early on and concentrating fine adjustments near the end is a much more sensible time allocation.

### 3.2 & 3.3 Two-Stage Non-Uniform Splitting
The integration interval $[1, 0]$ is split into $[1, \tau]$ and $[\tau, 0]$, with $\tau=0.3$ in practice. In the first stage (length 0.7), a single large Euler step maps noise state $x_1$ forward to generate a rough trajectory outline. In the second stage (length 0.3), the model directly predicts the average velocity from intermediate state $x_\tau$ to terminal state $0$, handling subtle action corrections and residual errors.

### 3.4 Terminal Refinement via SnapFlow and Joint Training
To predict the average velocity over $[\tau, 0]$, the authors adopt the SnapFlow shortcut learning mechanism. A stop-gradient is applied to the first-stage output $x_\tau$ to form $\tilde{x}_\tau$, and the network learns to match the ground-truth target average velocity $\bar{v}^*_{\tau\rightarrow 0}$ constructed from the teacher trajectory. During training, batches alternate between the standard Flow Matching branch and this two-stage branch with probability 0.5. At inference time, no teacher network is required, producing high-quality action chunks with just two network evaluations (2-NFE).

captions.F3: Trajectory analysis of the velocity field in standard 10-NFE Flow sampling. Velocity RMS on the left and adjacent-step angular deviations on the right clearly show that corrections concentrate near the end of denoising (steps 9–10).
captions.F4: Training and inference pipeline of the proposed two-stage non-uniform denoising. Rather than uniform steps, a non-uniform schedule of $1 \rightarrow 0.3 \rightarrow 0$ achieves coarse long-interval generation and fine short-interval refinement in just two steps.

sections.heading: Keeping Robots in Motion: A Distributed, Multi-Threaded Execution Engine
sections.summary: The authors built a distributed framework that decouples inference, action publication, and low-level robot control. It supports six real-time execution methods as interchangeable plugins on a shared platform, providing full tracing for inputs, outputs, and latency logs.
sections.details:
### 4.1 System Architecture
To prevent inference delays from disrupting robot control cycles, the distributed architecture loosely couples the robot client and GPU server. On the client side, dedicated threads run independently: an observation thread caches camera frames and joint states, an inference thread dispatches requests at a configurable rate, and an action-publication thread draws from an action buffer to stream commands to the arm at a steady frequency. Communication supports WebSockets, TCP sockets, or shared memory on a single machine.

### 4.2 Plugin Integration and Runtime Tracing
A key strength of this framework is that real-time control algorithms from prior work can be swapped in and evaluated over the exact same perception, buffer, and communication pipeline. Six methods were modularized: Naive Asynchronous (overwriting buffer with latest chunk), Temporal Smoothing (exponential moving average blending), Inference-time RTC (prefix conditioning at test time), Training-time RTC (latency simulation during training), Legato (training-time trajectory continuity injection), and VLASH (conditioning on predicted future handoff states). Complete timestamps and chunk provenance metadata are logged for every request and response, enabling system-level tracking of boundary behavior and discontinuity causes.

captions.F5: Architecture of the distributed real-time VLA inference and execution framework. Robot-side I/O and action publication run asynchronously alongside server-side VLA inference, supporting diverse real-time execution methods as modular plugins.

sections.heading: Bimanual Garment Folding: Real-Robot Benchmarks and 2-Step Flow
sections.summary: Six methods were compared on a 180-trial bimanual garment-folding task. Legato led among training-based methods (96.7% success), while Temporal Smoothing led among training-free methods (76.7%). Pairing either method with the 2-step Flow preserved strong success rates while drastically reducing inference time.
sections.details:
### 5.1 Real-Time Execution Comparison
Evaluations were conducted on an Agilex Piper dual-arm robot (14 DoF) performing a long-horizon task: unfolding a crumpled T-shirt and folding it three times. Three garments of varying sizes and colors were used across 30 trials per method (180 physical trials in total).

- **Task Performance**: Legato ranked highest with a 96.7% success rate (29/30), an average completion time of 73.56 s, and throughput of 47.31 folds/hr. VLASH followed closely at 93.3%. Among training-free methods, Temporal Smoothing was best at 76.7%. In contrast, Naive Asynchronous (53.3%) and RTC variants (50.0%–63.3%) struggled. Increasing the replanning rate to 3 Hz for Inference-time RTC did not improve its success rate, showing that faster replanning alone is insufficient.
- **Action Smoothness**: Legato achieved the lowest Tail Gap (0.0193 rad) and Switch Gap (0.0062 rad) across chunk transitions. Conversely, Naive Asynchronous produced violent transition shocks with peak acceleration reaching 744.1 rad/s². Temporal Smoothing capped peak acceleration at 25.6 rad/s² despite having larger boundary gaps, demonstrating that local low-pass filtering and trajectory-level continuity address different aspects of motion quality.

### 5.2 Evaluating Two-Stage 2-NFE Denoising
On an RTX 4090 D, the proposed 2-NFE method cut inference time from 61.56 ms (standard 10-NFE) to 21.96 ms—a 64.3% reduction (2.80× speedup). Offline joint and end-effector position errors remained closely comparable.

When combined with Legato and Temporal Smoothing on the physical robot, the 21.96 ms inference time held up well, delivering an 86.7% success rate with Legato and 70.0% with Temporal Smoothing. This confirms a compelling trade-off: major compute savings with only a minor drop in task success.

captions.F9: Local trajectory of joint 3 under Naive Asynchronous execution. Around 107 seconds, switching to a new chunk introduces an abrupt position jump and velocity reset, causing peak acceleration to spike to 744.09 rad/s².

sections.heading: The Real-Time VLA Landscape: Organizing Six Lines of Research
sections.summary: Prior research on real-time VLAs is categorized into six paradigms: asynchronous alignment, inter-chunk continuity, adaptive horizons, fast generation, continuous-time representations, and runtime correction. This paper provides a unified reference point for evaluating them fairly.
sections.details:
Efforts to bring VLAs into real-time real-world control fall into six primary directions:

- **Asynchronous Inference and Execution-Time Alignment**: Running inference concurrently with execution by fixing the executing prefix (RTC) or conditioning the policy on predicted handoff states (VLASH, FutureRTC).
- **Inter-Chunk Continuity and Action Priors**: Mitigating mode-switching jumps caused by independent sampling, either via past-trajectory guidance (BID) or by embedding continuity priors into model initialization and training (Legato, SEAM, ChunkFlow).
- **Adaptive Execution Horizons and Multi-Rate Control**: Modulating execution chunk length based on uncertainty or task phase (AAC, PACE), or pairing high- and low-rate policies hierarchically (HiPolicy).
- **Fast Action Generation and Streaming**: Single- or few-step action generation (Consistency Policy, SnapFlow), generating initial actions first (FASTER), and pipelining token generation with execution (StreamingVLA).
- **Continuous-Time Representations and Physical Feasibility**: Formulating actions via DCT frequency components or B-splines to guarantee trajectory smoothness without inflating output dimensionality at high control rates (FAST, BEAST, ABPolicy).
- **Runtime Correction and System Integration**: Correcting low-rate VLA outputs with fast auxiliary heads (A2C2), or building full-stack hardware-software pipelines with sensor delay calibration and buffer management (Realtime-VLA V2).

By placing representative methods from asynchronous alignment and inter-chunk continuity under one roof, this work offers a standardized experimental baseline.

sections.heading: Conclusions and Next Steps: Harmonizing Model and System Timing
sections.summary: Analyzing real-world VLA latency from both model and system standpoints yielded a 2.8× inference speedup via two-step non-uniform denoising and thorough physical robot validation. The findings underscore the need to co-optimize model computational efficiency with robot execution timing.
sections.details:
This study tackled the timing gap between slow VLA inference and fast robot control through a three-pronged effort: end-to-end latency measurement, model-level inference acceleration, and system-level real-robot evaluation.

Capturing the terminal-heavy correction behavior of Flow Matching velocity fields inspired two-stage non-uniform denoising ($1 \rightarrow 0.3 \rightarrow 0$). This reduced function evaluations from 10 to 2 and slashed inference time from 61.56 ms to 21.96 ms. Concurrently, a decoupled distributed framework enabled rigorous benchmarking of six real-time control methods across 180 bimanual garment-folding trials. The experiments established the superiority of Legato among training-based methods and Temporal Smoothing among training-free options, while showing that both integrate effectively with the 2-step denoising scheme.

Promising directions for future work include extending non-uniform sampling strategies to world-action models and exploring adaptive scheduling that dynamically adjusts inference rates and sampling steps based on scene dynamics and task phases.

takeaways: Real-world VLA latency stems not only from model inference but heavily from perception, image transfer, and actuator response (totaling nearly 80 ms), requiring holistic model-and-system solutions.

Because Flow Matching velocity fields remain stable through early stages and concentrate directional changes near the end, a non-uniform two-step schedule (one large step + one fine terminal step) is highly effective.

Simply increasing replanning frequency (e.g., to 3 Hz) does not guarantee higher success; enforcing chunk-boundary geometric continuity and state consistency (as in Legato) is critical for physical tasks.

Temporal Smoothing provides an effective, plug-and-play training-free option for trajectory smoothing, while Legato delivers the best balance of task success and dynamic continuity among training-based approaches.
limitations: Aggressively compressing denoising to 2 steps yields a 2.8× speedup, but incurs a modest performance drop of several to ten percentage points in task success rate.
Hyperparameters such as the split time $\tau=0.3$ and loss weighting terms are statically chosen, rather than dynamically adjusted based on task progress or environmental conditions.
Camera hardware clock synchronization and wrist-camera timing discrepancies still rely on individual offline calibration procedures.
